title: India's Cruellest Bargain: Millions of Workers Are Training the AI Systems That Will Replace Them
excerpt: From Infosys engineers whose code is now auto-generated to gig workers labelling data for $3 an hour, India's $315 billion IT sector is discovering that the machines it helps build don't need it anymore.
body:
At 9:47 on a recent morning in Bangalore, an Infosys engineer typed a few sentences in plain English into the company’s internal VibeCoder tool and pressed enter. By 10:17, she had a working prototype — frontend, backend, database schema, API endpoints, payment flow. Two years ago, that would have taken a team of four engineers three weeks. The tool she used was built, in part, by engineers whose jobs it is now designed to eliminate.

## The Loop

This is the defining paradox of India’s relationship with artificial intelligence in 2026: the country’s workers are simultaneously building the systems that make their own labour obsolete, and being paid — sometimes well — to do it.

The numbers are stark. India’s IT services industry, which employs 5.4 million workers and contributes $315 billion to the economy — roughly 8 per cent of GDP — is undergoing structural cuts that have nothing to do with recession. TCS let go of approximately 12,000 employees in a recent tranche. Infosys scaled back campus hiring by 20 to 25 per cent. Wipro and HCL trimmed bench strength. India’s GDP is growing at 6 to 7 per cent. The cuts are structural, not cyclical. AI simply made headcount less necessary.

Meanwhile, a parallel economy has emerged. Companies like Mercor — a $10 billion San Francisco startup backed by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta — pay professionals $90 an hour to train AI systems. The work is intellectually demanding: doctors teach diagnostic models, lawyers feed contracts into systems that will read them faster, social workers coach chatbots to de-escalate family crises. Mercor pays out more than $2 million per day to its contractors. The money is real. So is the trajectory: these workers are monetising their expertise on the way down.

## The Data Labelling Underclass

At the other end of the pay scale, a vast workforce of Indian data labellers earns between $3 and $15 an hour on platforms like Remotasks, Scale AI, and Outlier. They label images, rank chatbot responses, correct AI hallucinations, and flag disturbing content. They are not building AI — they are feeding it, one tagged data point at a time. And when the models they train become accurate enough, the demand for their labour will evaporate.

A recent investigation into America’s AI labour ecosystem found that many workers training AI systems for companies connected to OpenAI and Google are living paycheque to paycheque. Some are on food stamps. Nearly one in five have experienced homelessness. The pattern extends to India, where data annotation has become the new call centre — a gateway to the global economy that offers employment without security, income without trajectory.

The irony is precise. India’s first great outsourcing boom in the 2000s was built on the premise that the country could provide skilled labour cheaply. AI is now outsourcing the outsourcers. The code-writing that employed millions of Indians is being automated by tools those Indians helped build. The data labelling that trains those tools pays a fraction of what the original coding jobs did.

## What Survives

Not all of India’s IT workforce is doomed. The engineers who will survive the transition are what industry observers call “bilinguals” — people who understand both code and business domains, who can articulate problems rather than merely implement solutions. AI, for all its speed, still makes catastrophic mistakes. It needs human judgment, context, and taste — qualities that cannot be extracted into labelled data points.

India’s IT leadership knows this. Infosys, TCS, and Wipro are all investing in AI-native training programmes, reorienting their workforces from code production to problem articulation. But retraining 5.4 million workers is a generational project, and AI is moving at quarterly speed.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For the Indian diaspora, the implications are immediate. H-1B visa holders working in US tech companies are watching entry-level postings in AI-exposed roles fall by 48 per cent since 2022. Recent graduates are submitting an average of 23 applications per open position. The path that brought hundreds of thousands of Indians to Silicon Valley — study engineering, get hired by a tech company, work your way up — is narrowing in real time.

Some are adapting. Indian-origin founders are disproportionately represented in the current Y Combinator cohort. Stanford’s StartX accelerator reports that 35 per cent of its 2026 cohort are current undergraduates who deferred graduation to build companies. The entrepreneurial instinct that built India’s IT industry in the first place may be its best defence against the machines that industry created.

But for the millions of Indian workers who are not founders — the mid-career engineers, the fresh graduates, the gig workers labelling data at 3 AM — the question is more existential. The highest-paid work in their field has become teaching AI to make them unnecessary. The industry they built is being dismantled by the tools they trained. And the bargain they struck — expertise in exchange for stability — is being rewritten in code they can no longer negotiate.
author: Diaspora Desk
